claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 as synthesized has a well-defined hierarchical heterostructure containing ordered and disordered phase regions.
A physics-informed surrogate model can use mesoscale phase distributions and interfacial order parameters to predict HfNbTiVAl10 mechanical behavior.
The surrogate model can reduce computational time by roughly 50% relative to established full-scale finite-element simulations.
The surrogate model can predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior with error below approximately 10%.
Phase fraction, grain-boundary characteristics, and interfacial-bonding cues can serve as surrogate-model inputs.
Mesoscale phase distribution and ordered interfaces mediate dislocation activity in HfNbTiVAl10.
Mesoscale phase distribution and ordered interfaces mediate crack initiation and propagation in HfNbTiVAl10.
Hierarchical ordering can activate multiple dislocation-slip and fault-related mechanisms that affect tensile strength and ductility.
The hierarchical microstructure encodes scale-bridging features that govern deformation and failure responses in HfNbTiVAl10.
Embedding selected structural mediators in a simplified model can capture essential deformation mechanisms without full multiphysics computational overhead.
Embedding selected structural mediators in a simplified model can capture essential fracture mechanisms without full multiphysics computational overhead.
The predicted mechanical-property error will be below approximately 10% relative to experimental results.
The surrogate will require approximately half the computational time of conventional simulation methods.
Conventional full-scale multiphysics finite-element simulations capture detailed microstructural behavior.
Conventional full-scale multiphysics finite-element simulations require significantly greater computational resources and time.
The approach may fail when the microstructure is poorly resolved or differs substantially from its assumed hierarchical ordering.
The approach may fail when abnormal segregation or phase instability dominates the mechanical response.
Predictive accuracy and efficiency gains may depend on microstructural-characterization fidelity and the range of loading conditions.
Independent tensile and fracture measurements can test the model against both experiments and conventional simulations.
Failure to achieve both a ±10% experimental error margin and at least a 50% computational-efficiency gain would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis initially describes the below-10% error as a comparison with established finite-element simulations, whereas the predicted outcome and falsification rule define the error relative to experiments. These are different reference standards.
